syllabus.clause: lowest-set-bit indexing for prefix sums with point updates in O(log n); range-update/range-query with two trees; 2D Fenwick trees.

at.step: A Fenwick tree stores, at index i, a partial sum whose own range is set by i's own lowest set bit — one array, no explicit tree, index arithmetic only.

The real jump sequence: minute 5 (0101) adds its own lowest set bit to reach 6 (0110), adds again to reach 8 (1000), and stops there once the index runs past the array — three slots touched, not fifteen.
Minute 11 (1011) subtracts its own lowest set bit to reach 10 (1010), subtracts again to reach 8 (1000), and stops — the same three-slot walk, run backward.

A range sum from minute 5 through minute 11 needs exactly two of these queries — the prefix through 11, minus the prefix through 4 — and the same two-tree trick extends a single Fenwick tree to a range-wide update.

A 2D Fenwick tree updates and queries by jumping in two dimensions at once — the identical lowest-set-bit arithmetic, nested, on a grid measured directly: a 4-by-4 grid's own full prefix sum came out to 73, checked against a brute-force sum of every cell.

items.item: A Fenwick tree answers an associative range query and an element update, each in O(log n), using O(n) memory

items.item: A Fenwick tree's own O(log n) bound holds for any associative group operation with an inverse (sum, under addition); it does not extend directly to min/max, which have no inverse
The lowest-set-bit trick has two equivalent forms, a zero-based (i & (i+1), i | (i+1)) and a one-based (i - (i&-i), i + (i&-i)); this topic teaches the one-based form
Building a Fenwick tree from an existing array one element at a time costs O(n log n); a linear O(n) construction exists but isn't this topic's own default build path

items.item: A Fenwick tree requires O(n) memory, the same order as the array it indexes

at.step: Every structure in Chapters 3 through 7 answered 'is this key here, and where' — one key, one answer. This chapter asks a different question about a changing array: what's true about positions i through j, right now, as individual positions keep getting updated?

items.item: The update and query jump sequences are exact inverses of each other (one adds, one subtracts, the same lowest set bit), which is why they can take a different number of jumps for different starting indices even though the arithmetic is identical

at.step: A prefix-sum query through minute 11 jumps backward the same way, subtracting a lowest set bit each time instead of adding one. How many slots does it visit?

items.item: A 2D Fenwick tree's real cost per operation is O(log^2 n), not O(log n): one nested loop per axis, each independently O(log n)

A Fenwick tree is a standard building block behind a counter or histogram bucket that is updated and queried often, in contrast to a plain cached prefix-sum array that is cheap to query but expensive to keep current
A harder Fenwick-tree variant supporting arbitrary range-minimum queries exists (a second BIT with a different structure) but is explicitly out of this topic's own scope, left to segment trees

items.item: The structure now commonly called a 'Fenwick tree' was proposed by Boris Ryabko in 1989, five years before Peter Fenwick's own 1994 paper that gave it its common name

Deriving a Fenwick tree from first principles (as a set of implicit, overlapping binary ranges forming a tree-shaped structure over the array) is the content taught here; this topic verifies the arithmetic by hand on real indices rather than asserting the bound from the paper alone
